title: Cloudflare cut its AI review bill by two thirds and kept the findings
dek: One team's code-review agents went from $2.43 to $0.77 a review by fixing caching, trimming tools and choosing models by test. Also: Meta's deliberately dumb orchestrator, skills that crowd each other out, and studios hiding demos from cloners.

theme.mood: a practical Tuesday about paying less for the same work

tldr.text: Cloudflare's multi-agent code reviewer now costs **$0.77 a review, down 68%**. Most of the drop came from cache hits, fewer tool calls and model choices tested on real reviews.
Meta keeps its agent router **deliberately thin**: 1,300 lines, seven fixed steps, and only one step that asks a model anything.
Load two agent skills for the same job and models follow one and quietly drop the other: rule adherence fell from **93-99% to about 61%** in a new benchmark.
The studio behind Moonlighter swapped a public playtest for a closed Discord test, citing **games cloned before launch**, as Steam Next Fest runs to October 26.

blocks.title: Cloudflare cut its AI code review bill by 68%
blocks.gist: Cloudflare runs a team of AI agents that reviews its engineers' code changes. Over a few weeks it cut the average cost per review from $2.43 to $0.77, and checked that the useful findings did not go away.
body: The reviewer is several agents: a coordinator that hands each code change to specialists for code quality, security, performance, documentation and compliance. Costs had crept up from $1.19 a review in April to about $2.46 by late August, so one engineer went through the bill line by line.

The biggest single fix was caching. Every reviewer's first request now starts with the same block of tool definitions and shared rules, so the provider can reuse it instead of charging full price again. Then came a series of small cuts: removing tools reviewers could not use, skipping reviewers on re-reviews that did not need them, stopping as soon as the review was posted, and killing cancelled jobs that kept running.

Model choices were tested, not assumed. A split test found the newer mid-size model 47% to 62% cheaper per run, so all those reviewers moved to it. Of the $1.67 saved per review, $0.65 came from code changes and $1.06 from model and effort settings.

stat.label: average cost per review, down from $2.43

blocks.why: Agent pipelines in CI are billed per token, and most of that bill is often re-sent context. Measuring whether the first request hits the cache, then testing cheaper settings against a quality metric, is a playbook any team can copy.
blocks.forYou: The same levers apply to your routines and subagent-heavy sessions: put the stable rules and tool list first, drop tools a subagent never uses, and check cache reads on the first request in your API usage before touching models.

terms.def: Reusing the start of a request the model provider has already processed, which is billed at a fraction of the normal price.
Sending a random half of real jobs to each option and comparing the results, so the difference comes from the option and not the jobs.
A setting that controls how much a model thinks before answering; more effort costs more tokens.

deep: Cost history as reported: $1.19 per review in April, about $2.46 by late August, $2.43 averaged over the two most expensive weeks, $0.77 now. Median review time fell from 4m 09s to 1m 32s. The shared cached prefix (September 16) took cost per review from $2.47 to $2.02 on its own; the call-trimming changes of September 21 to 23 saved about $0.20 more, including about $0.07 per job from stopping once the review is posted.

Three sub-reviewers share one first request: the first writes the cache and the other two wait up to 20 seconds to read it, saving about nine cents per reviewer. The coordinator moved to Opus 5.5 at medium effort; Sonnet reviewers moved from Sonnet 5 to Sonnet 5.5 after a split test; code quality runs at high effort, adding about two cents per review. The reviewer runs on OpenCode v2.

Quality checks: a finding counted as acted on if its flagged lines changed in the author's next push (a baseline of nearby lines changed about 15% of the time). Serious code quality findings acted on rose from 34% to 59%. Two models from different providers judged 657 findings blind: important findings per review went from 0.28 to 0.30, and findings judged too severe fell from 0.46 to 0.14 per review. Medium effort did lose real performance findings (about 64% fewer important ones), and the author notes the before and after steps are not a controlled experiment.

sources.label: Cloudflare: Cutting our inference bill by 68%

image.alt: Line chart of weekday cost per review, September 7 to October 6: it falls from about $2.45 to $0.75, with eight numbered changes marked, from a shared cached prefix to the Sonnet 5.5 rollout.

blocks.title: Meta made its agent router dumber, and the agents got more reliable
blocks.gist: Meta built a system of 14 specialist AI agents for data pipeline work, and found it worked best when the program that routes work between them does almost no thinking itself.
blocks.intro: The orchestrator is about 1,300 lines and runs a fixed seven-step protocol for 20+ kinds of request. Six steps are ordinary code; only the hand-off asks a model to reason. Domain knowledge lives in 25+ files the specialists load when they need them.

nodes.label: Request
nodes.note: add a column, add an event, migrate a pipeline

nodes.label: Fixed checks
nodes.note: read the agent's instructions, confirm the target, gather and infer fields

nodes.label: Reliability gate
nodes.note: active warnings and required reviewers, checked in code

nodes.label: Delegate
nodes.note: the only step where a model reasons

nodes.label: Specialist agent
nodes.note: its own context and knowledge files, one of 14

nodes.label: Handle result
nodes.note: surface errors, move to the next phase

blocks.caption: The seven-step protocol from Meta's write-up, with steps 1 to 4 folded into one box. Workflow templates decide which specialists run in which order.
blocks.why: When one agent holds every rule for a big system, it starts mixing conventions up. Keeping the router as plain code and pushing knowledge into small, separately loaded specialists is a pattern any agent setup can borrow.
blocks.forYou: This maps directly onto skills and subagents: a thin top-level command that only routes, specialist subagents with their own instruction files, and knowledge in files loaded on demand. Pipeline migration was added as a new template with no new agent code.

terms.def: The program that receives a request, decides which agent should handle each part, and collects the results.
Everything a model can see while it works: instructions, files and earlier messages.
Fixed sequences that say which specialists run, in what order, for a kind of request.

deep: Results Meta reports: preparing the configuration for a new data column took three to four days by hand, about a day with the earlier config-driven system, and under an hour now. About two thirds of changes land without significant human edits. A results table lists about 70% success without per-task prompt engineering, a production revert rate of about 0.2%, 1,282 code changes landed and 1,384 columns processed.

Why not one agent: Meta says a single agent's accuracy fell as its context grew, because it confused conventions across subsystems. A single-agent design reached 70% to 80% success only with a custom prompt for each task, and 10% to 20% without. The post cites a separate preprint that measured 65.3% accuracy for orchestrated agents against 16.6% for a single agent on 80-task batches.

Workflow templates are state machines: column onboarding has four phases, event onboarding and pipeline migration five each. A column can touch up to six pipeline stages across three repositories, with Python configs that drive C++ code generation.

blocks.title: A cheap grader can stand in for a big one, if you tune it
blocks.gist: Hamel Husain and Antaripa Saha tested small yes-or-no classifier models as graders for AI outputs, and found the cheapest one close behind at a fraction of the price once its cut-off was tuned.

stats.label: F1 score of the best grader on 98 labeled traces
cheaper for the runner-up, at F1 0.79

body: The default pass mark of 0.5 can be badly wrong; they pick it per model with cross-validation, then check whether the scores match real failure rates. The dataset is small, so treat it as a method, not a ranking.
blocks.why: Automated graders run on every change, so their price adds up. Tuning the threshold costs no new model calls and can make a cheaper grader good enough.
blocks.forYou: If you grade agent output with a model in CI, save the scores once and sweep the threshold before paying for a bigger judge.

terms.def: A single number from 0 to 1 that balances how many real failures a grader catches and how many of its alarms are real.
The score above which the grader's answer counts as a fail.
Testing a choice on several held-out slices of the data so it is not tuned to one lucky sample.

deep: Numbers from the post: OpenAI Decisions (GPT-6 Luna) reached F1 0.87 at 3.72 cents per 100 runs; Perplexity Decider 1.1 27B reached 0.79 at 0.82 cents. They set a floor of 80% precision and recall, used stratified 5-fold cross-validation with the same splits for every model, and tried Platt scaling for calibration, which helped some models and slightly worsened OpenAI's Brier score (0.159 to 0.164).

sources.label: Hamel Husain: How to use decision models for evals

blocks.title: Two skills for one job: the agent follows one and drops the other
blocks.gist: Researchers loaded two instruction packs written for the same task into AI models and found the models usually obeyed one pack fully and silently ignored the other, even when the rules did not conflict.
body: Agent skills are packaged instructions that people share and install, so two written by different authors for the same job, say commit messages, can easily load together. The SkillClash benchmark tested 16 such pairs, each skill with six checkable rules and one worked example, on seven models from 4B open models to GPT-4.1.

A skill alone was followed 93% to 99% of the time. Add a second skill for the same job and adherence fell to about 61%, mostly as takeover: one skill's rules all kept, the other's all dropped. An unrelated second skill changed nothing. Telling the model which skill wins did not bring the dropped one back.
points: The worked examples drive it: an example that follows both skills cut takeover to 1% to 15% on six models.
One merged skill file reached 96% to 99% of achievable rules on all seven models.
The test skills were written for the benchmark; a reanalysis of real-skill data shows a smaller effect of about 8 points.
blocks.why: As teams install skills from many sources, overlaps are easy to miss, and the failure is silent: the output looks fine but half the rules are gone.
blocks.forYou: Check your global and project skills for pairs that cover the same job, such as commit messages or PR descriptions, and merge them. Today's Try this walks through it.

terms.def: Folders of instructions and examples an AI agent loads when a task matches them.
A sample input and the ideal output, included so the model can copy the pattern.
The paper's name for when one skill's rules are all followed and the other's are all dropped.

deep: SkillClash (arXiv 2610.25064, submitted October 18) by Parsa Razmara, Seyedarmin Azizi and Ardalan Aryashad. Models ranged from Qwen3-4B and Phi-4 mini to Qwen3-235B and GPT-4.1. An "apply both" instruction helped only the two strongest models, and only about 21% to 22% of their outputs were fully correct. The merged file was written by Claude Opus 5.5; 68% to 94% of outputs with it were fully correct, and much of the gain came from its single worked example, which helps only when the example itself is right. Code is on GitHub.

image.alt: Bar chart: seven models follow about 93 to 99 percent of a skill's rules alone or beside an unrelated skill, and about 61 percent beside a second skill for the same job. Heat maps show one skill's rules winning.

blocks.title: Claude Code 2.1.304: a security check for hosted agents and a safer worktree exit
blocks.gist: A large update to Anthropic's coding agent adds a command that checks hosted agent settings against Anthropic's security guide, fixes a way work could be lost on exit, and warns before costly session resumes.
blocks.intro: Version 2.1.303 was bug fixes only. Version 2.1.304, released October 19, is the one to read.

items.title: Security check for Managed Agents
items.text: `/claude-api managed-agents-secure` compares a hosted agent's settings with Anthropic's published security guide and lists the differences. It changes nothing.

items.title: Worktree exit no longer deletes your branch
items.text: `claude --worktree` used to remove the worktree and its branch without asking at exit when the checkout was detached or on another branch, which could lose commits.

items.title: Guided auto mode setup
items.text: `/auto-mode-setup` reads your project and recent sessions to teach auto mode about your environment, now also on Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry.

items.title: Warning before an expensive resume
items.text: Pro and Max users are warned when resuming an idle conversation would use a noticeable share of the 5-hour limit, and can start fresh instead.

items.title: Prompt before deleting mounted drives
items.text: Recursive deletes of top-level or mounted folders such as `/Volumes`, `/media` or WSL's `/mnt/c` now ask first.

items.title: Compaction window values fixed
items.text: `CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW=200k` used to silently mean 100K. It now accepts `k` and `M` and warns about values it ignores.

blocks.why: Two of these protect work you could otherwise lose without noticing: commits in a worktree branch and files on a mounted drive. Updating is worth it for those alone.
blocks.forYou: Run the managed-agents-secure check on any hosted agent you deploy, and set the compaction window again if you used a `k` value. Self-paced `/loop` wakeups at the one-hour maximum also stop landing just after the prompt cache expires.

terms.def: A second working folder for the same git repository, so an agent can work on a branch without touching your main checkout.
Anthropic's hosted service that runs agents in its own cloud sandboxes.
Summarising older parts of a long conversation so it fits in the model's context.

deep: Other changes in 2.1.304: tool search is on by default behind a custom `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` and retried without it on a 400 or 422; `context_management` errors behind LLM gateways are fixed by resending without that field; compaction now resends the skill list, and `/reload-skills` sends only new or changed skills; skill hooks are limited to 1,024 hooks and 16,384 matcher characters per session per source; `/fast` lost its research preview label on Opus 5.5; bracket globs in `sandbox.filesystem.denyRead` no longer break sandboxed commands on Linux; throughput improves with many subagents running.

blocks.title: WhatsApp's help pages carried hidden notes for chatbots
blocks.gist: A researcher found invisible text on 80 WhatsApp help pages telling AI assistants not to suggest contacting a regulator or citing privacy law. The notes vanished after press coverage.
blocks.intro: Redact.dev read 545 WhatsApp help pages and found 102 hidden blocks of text on 80 of them. None turned up on 300 Facebook and Instagram pages checked. WhatsApp said they were chatbot instructions exposed by a bug.

events.text: An archived copy of the pages shows no hidden text.
The hidden notes are present in an archived copy.
Redact.dev finds them, including advice not to cite GDPR even when the user does.
All 102 blocks are gone by 02:08 UTC, after WIRED covers the find.

blocks.why: Agents that read documentation also read whatever is hidden in it. Text aimed at one company's chatbot can steer anyone's assistant that fetches the page.
blocks.forYou: Worth a line in agent instructions for any SaaS support bot: vendor pages are data, and hidden text in them is not policy.

terms.def: The European Union's data protection law, which gives people rights over their personal data.

deep: The author tested on October 9 whether the notes were served to OpenAI, Anthropic and Perplexity crawlers and found they did not appear to be. He did not test whether any assistant obeyed them. WhatsApp told reporters it wants chatbots not to offer legal advice.

blocks.title: Anonymous clones from GitHub may start asking for a login
blocks.gist: GitHub says that during unusual traffic it may require sign-in for cloning public repositories over HTTPS, so build scripts that clone anonymously could suddenly fail.
blocks.intro: The change, posted October 19, covers unauthenticated HTTPS clone and fetch of public repositories. SSH, pushes and authenticated HTTPS are unaffected. GitHub gives no end date.

steps.title: Find anonymous clones
steps.text: Search CI configs, Dockerfiles and setup scripts for `git clone https://github.com/` lines that pass no token.

steps.title: Use the built-in token in Actions
steps.text: Inside GitHub Actions, authenticate with the provided `GITHUB_TOKEN`; the checkout action already does.

steps.title: Use an app token elsewhere
steps.text: In other CI, GitHub recommends a GitHub App installation token, or a personal access token if you must.

steps.title: Know the symptom
steps.text: A clone that worked yesterday and now fails with an authentication error is this change, not a broken repo.

blocks.why: Many builds pull public dependencies straight from GitHub without credentials. They are the ones that will break, and only some of the time.
blocks.forYou: Check the deploy workflows and any agent sandbox setup scripts that clone public repos anonymously.

terms.def: Continuous integration: servers that build and test code automatically on every change.
A secure way to connect to a server using a key pair instead of a password.

sources.label: GitHub Changelog: Git over HTTPS may require authentication

blocks.title: Studios start hiding demos from cloners
blocks.gist: The studio behind Moonlighter scaled its next game's public playtest down to a closed Discord test, worried that AI tools let others copy a game before it ships.
blocks.quote: With launch still months away, a large public build of ReVamp felt like too big a risk.
blocks.speaker: Digital Sun Games
blocks.context: Digital Sun cited news of games being reverse-engineered, cloned and published before the original is out. Its closed test starts October 29. Game Developer reports developers describe feeding demos and trailers into AI tools to rebuild core features, and notes that game mechanics have little copyright protection.
blocks.why: Public demos are how small studios get found. If showing a build means risking a copy that launches first, studios face a real trade-off between reach and protection.
blocks.forYou: Browser builds are the easiest to lift whole. For the web games, think about what a public build exposes (source maps, unminified code, raw assets) before the next playtest.

sources.label: Game Developer: Moonlighter developer delays public playtest

blocks.title: A forest floor material in 16 layers, roots first
blocks.gist: An artist explained how they built a realistic, repeating forest floor texture in Substance 3D Designer, spending almost half the week on the tree roots alone.
blocks.intro: Zeqi Mu's breakdown for 80 Level took about a week. The order of work is the lesson: structure first, detail last.

steps.title: Build the roots first
steps.text: The first three days went into a root system made of splines scattered along other splines, which gave control over density and thickness.

steps.title: Stack layers bottom to top
steps.text: Sixteen layers: roots, stones from large to tiny, moss, dead leaves, twigs, clover, lichen, branches, grass, fallen leaves and ferns.

steps.title: Generate stones as shapes
steps.text: Stones come from a splatter node in distance-field mode with random roundness and facet count, so no two look the same.

steps.title: Take moss normals from its own layer
steps.text: Moss surface detail comes from its splatter, not the combined height, so it stays crisp on top of everything else.

steps.title: Keep big shapes sparse
steps.text: Low density on the main roots hides the repeat when the texture tiles across a large ground.

blocks.why: Tiling ground materials cover most of an outdoor scene. Fixing the large shapes before adding detail is what keeps the repeat from showing.
blocks.forYou: Useful reference for world-tool demo scenes: sparse large features are what hide tiling on big terrain.

terms.def: Smooth curves defined by a few control points, used here to draw roots.
Repeats seamlessly side by side, so one small texture can cover a large surface.
Per-pixel directions that tell the renderer which way a surface faces, faking fine bumps.

deep: Tools named in the breakdown: Scatter Splines on Splines (Cells 2 was tried and dropped for roots), multiplied Gaussian noises for height, Shape Splatter v2 in SDF mode. In Unreal Engine 5 the material uses Nanite displacement and a subsurface scattering mask on the clover leaves; Marmoset Toolbag was used for presentation.

sources.label: 80 Level: Making a tileable forest floor material

image.alt: Two spheres wrapped in the finished forest floor material: thick tree roots over soil, stones, moss, clover and dead leaves.

learn.question: What does an orchestrator do in a team of AI agents?
learn.answer: An orchestrator is the part of a multi-agent system that takes a request, decides which specialist agent should handle it, passes along what that agent needs, and collects the result. It manages the work rather than doing it.
learn.analogy: Like a restaurant's expediter: they read each ticket, call it to the right station, check plates before they leave, and never cook anything themselves.
body: One agent with every rule for a large system tends to mix things up as its context fills. Splitting the work among specialists, each with its own instructions and a small context, keeps each one focused. Something then has to route requests and check results: that is the orchestrator.

Today's stories show two styles. Meta's orchestrator is plain code with one model call, so it behaves the same every time. Cloudflare's reviewer uses a model as its coordinator and had to tune which model and effort level that coordinator runs at. Either way, the orchestrator decides what each specialist sees, which is also where much of the cost goes.

nodes.label: Classify
nodes.note: what kind of request is this?

nodes.label: Check
nodes.note: gates before and after the work

nodes.label: Gather
nodes.note: fields and context the specialist needs

tryThis.title: Merge two agent skills that do the same job
tryThis.gist: Find skills that overlap, fold them into one file with one correct example, and stop half your rules from being silently dropped.
tryThis.needs: A coding agent that loads skills, such as Claude Code, with more than a handful installed.

steps.title: List your skills
steps.text: Look in the project's `.claude/skills/` and your personal `~/.claude/skills/`, plus any installed by plugins. Note what job each one claims in its description.

steps.title: Find same-job pairs
steps.text: Flag any two that cover the same task: commit messages, pull request descriptions, bug reports, changelogs. The study found an unrelated second skill did no harm; same-job pairs did.

steps.title: Merge into one rule list
steps.text: Write one `SKILL.md` with every rule you want to keep from both, resolving real conflicts yourself. Do not rely on a "this skill takes priority" line; it did not help in the study.

steps.title: Write one example that obeys every rule
steps.text: End the file with a single worked example and check it against each rule by hand. A wrong example spreads its mistakes.

steps.title: Remove the originals and compare
steps.text: Disable the two old skills, then run the same five prompts and count how many rules from each original show up in the output.

tryThis.check: Rules from both original skills appear in the output, not just one skill's set. In the paper the merged file kept 96% to 99% of achievable rules, against about 61% for the clashing pair.

terms.def: The file in a skill's folder that holds its description, instructions and examples.

tryThis.forYou: Start with the skills that write commits and PR descriptions across the plugin and SaaS repos; those are the likeliest to overlap with plugin-installed ones.

sparks.signal: 145 points and 108 comments on Hacker News on October 19.
sparks.hook: A 4B Qwen3 tune trained on a laptop cuts the author's count of AI-style phrases from 121 to 12.5 per 1,000 words, by his own measure.

sparks.title: Mac.apk runs Android apps as normal Mac apps
sparks.signal: 288 points and 155 comments on Hacker News, 804 GitHub stars, on October 19.

sparks.forYou: A quick check for the Flutter apps: does the Android build run under it, and faster than the emulator?

sparks.title: Lemmings for PalmOS, source released

lab.title: SWE-Residual: Evaluating Starting-State Robustness of Coding Agents
lab.headline: Hand a coding agent a repo that a previous agent wrongly called done, and it often calls it done too.
lab.authors: Jinze Li, Weijie Liu, Jinfeng Xu et al. (HKU, UBC, University of Tokyo, Tencent and others)
lab.problem: Benchmarks start agents from a clean repo. In practice an agent often picks up half-finished or wrong work left by an earlier run that claimed success.
lab.idea: Build 198 starting states from 111 tasks by keeping the code that earlier agents submitted as complete but that fails hidden tests. Give a new agent only the original request and that state, with no hint that anything failed.
lab.result: Success fell 20.6 to 53.5 points against a clean start: on DeepSWE, GPT-6-Sol dropped from 65.6% to 33.5% and Gemini-3.8-Flash from 72.2% to 20.0%. In 58.9% to 88.2% of failed continuations the same tests failed at the end as at the start. Model rankings flipped between the two conditions.
lab.useIt: When a fresh session picks up a branch, do not just say continue: give it the failing test output or tell it to re-run the tests first, or reset to a known good state.
lab.forYou: Matters for long routines that resume each other's work: start every resumed run by re-running the checks.

image.alt: Diagram of a failed earlier attempt, a clean start that succeeds and a residual start that fails, beside a bar chart where every model scores far lower from the residual start.

lab.title: StopLoss: Teaching Agents to Predict Failure and Stop Early
lab.headline: A small cheap model can watch a coding agent and stop runs that are going nowhere, cutting cost without losing solves.
lab.authors: Jiarong Liang, Xueguang Ma, Dongfu Jiang et al. (University of Waterloo)
lab.problem: Failing agent runs burn tokens until they hit a limit. Using a large model as a judge to stop them costs a lot and, here, also stopped runs that would have succeeded.
lab.idea: Fine-tune a 7B to 8B model on finished runs labelled by whether they passed. At checkpoints it reads the last three actions and results and scores the chance of failure; a threshold tuned on successful runs decides when to stop. The agent itself is unchanged.
lab.result: Cost per solved task fell 24.2% to 30.6% on SWE-bench Pro (48.1% with a Qwen3-8B monitor), while keeping 99.0% of solves on SWE-bench Verified, against 89.5% to 91.8% for GPT judges. Monitoring 425 runs cost $0.44, against $4.18 to $33.20 for the judges.
lab.useIt: The trained monitor needs your own labelled runs. The cheap first step is a hook that counts repeated failing tool calls and stops or escalates the run.
